items.title: Why Money.Add refuses to add USD to EUR
items.body:
A number without its currency is meaningless: 5000 USD plus 1000 EUR is not 6000 of anything. If `Add` simply summed the amounts, it would return 6000 labelled with the first value's currency, a wrong total that looks right. `Money.Add` instead compares the two currencies (ignoring case) and throws `InvalidOperationException("Money values must use the same currency.")` when they differ. The catalog: "Prevents adding USD to EUR." It also notes a gap: negative amounts are still allowed unless guarded elsewhere.

Why the others are wrong:
- `Add` has no exchange rate and converts nothing.
- It does no rounding; decimal precision is not the issue.
- Record equality is unaffected, and `Add` returns a new value (`this with { Amount = ... }`), not the first value unchanged.

excerpts.quote: if (!Currency.Equals(other.Currency, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) { throw new InvalidOperationException("Money values must use the same currency."); } return this with { Amount = Amount + other.Amount };
**Why it works:** Prevents adding USD to EUR. **Failure modes:** Allows negative amount unless separately guarded.

items.title: Why the three-month plan starts with security
items.body:
The critique's ranked plan begins: "Security first: auth, tenant scoping, and API integration tests." The risk table explains why: the missing auth boundary is rated High priority with High confidence, and the app handles workforce, payroll and compliance data. Nothing else matters much if anyone can read it. The rest follows in order: contract reliability, persistence migration, observability, frontend resilience.

Why the others are wrong:
- Structured logs and metrics are step 4 (observability), rated Low in the risk table.
- EF persistence is step 3.
- Generating TypeScript contracts is step 2, contract reliability.

excerpts.quote: 1. Security first: auth, tenant scoping, and API integration tests. Anchors: current unauthenticated controller at `src/PeblClone.Api/Controllers/WorkforceController.cs:6-40`.
High | No auth boundary

readMore.why: The full ranked plan and the migration strategy for each step.

items.title: Why a silent mock fallback is rated high risk
items.body:
`getDashboard` wraps the real request in `try`. On any error the `catch` returns `mockDashboard` with `source: 'mock'`. If the API is down in production, users still see a full, plausible dashboard and may not notice the outage, or may act on fake numbers. The catalog names the failure mode: "Production outage masked by mock data." The fix is to gate the fallback by environment and show explicit error states, adding the UI error state before disabling the fallback.

Why the others are wrong:
- The `catch` returns once; there is no retry loop.
- The guides do not say the mock contains real names or salaries.
- The fallback runs in the browser and cannot make the API return 500.

excerpts.quote: } catch { return { data: mockDashboard, source: 'mock' };
**Failure modes:** Production outage masked by mock data.
Mock fallback can hide outage

items.title: Why the schema ships first in a database migration
items.body:
Step 5 of the migration guidance reads: "Keep rollback possible: deploy schema, then code, then data changes." If the schema change goes first and is additive, the old code can keep running on it, so you can still roll the new code back. Data changes come last because they are the hardest to undo. The critique adds a second safety net: keep the in-memory adapter selectable by config.

Why the others are wrong:
- Removing the in-memory adapter first throws away the rollback path the critique wants to keep.
- A data migration or backfill first needs a schema to write into and is the hardest step to reverse.
- Code before schema means the new code would run against tables that do not exist yet.

excerpts.quote: 5. Keep rollback possible: deploy schema, then code, then data changes.
| Persistence | Add EF adapter behind existing port. | Existing application tests plus DB integration tests. | Keep in-memory adapter selectable by config. |

items.title: What a stable port buys when EF arrives
items.body:
Controllers and application services depend on the interface `IWorkforceReadModel`, not on the in-memory class. So adding EF means writing a new adapter that implements the same interface and changing the one registration line in `DependencyInjection.cs`. Nothing above the port has to change. The critique lists this as a strong choice: it "Allows persistence migration without changing controllers."

Why the others are wrong:
- The application tests stay useful; the persistence guide's drill even asks which existing tests should still pass with an EF adapter.
- Putting EF attributes on Domain entities is what the migration guidance says not to do ("without letting EF attributes leak into Domain").
- Swapping the adapter says nothing about moving seed data or dropping the old store; the critique wants the in-memory adapter kept selectable.

excerpts.quote: If EF is added, keep the application port stable at `src/PeblClone.Application/Workforce/IWorkforceReadModel.cs:5-12`. Replace `InMemoryWorkforceReadModel` with an EF adapter and update DI at `src/PeblClone.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:9-12`.
Allows persistence migration without changing controllers.
1. Add entities that map to domain concepts without letting EF attributes leak into Domain.

items.title: How RequiresAttention can become N+1 queries under EF
items.body:
`RequiresAttention` runs `ComplianceChecks.Any(...)` on each worker. Today the checks are already in memory. With EF Core, if `ComplianceChecks` is a navigation loaded lazily, touching it for each worker on the dashboard fires one extra SQL query per worker: 1 query for the workers plus N for their checks. That is the "N+1" failure the guide lists. It also notes the dashboard reads all workers with no paging, which makes N large.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing filters high-risk checks out in SQL; the filter is the C# expression on the record.
- EF does populate navigation collections (eagerly or lazily); the guide warns about how many queries that costs, not about nulls.
- The guide names no deadlock risk; these are read-only queries.

excerpts.quote: public bool RequiresAttention => Status == WorkerStatus.NeedsAttention || ComplianceChecks.Any(check => !check.IsResolved && check.RiskLevel is ComplianceRiskLevel.High);

- N+1: if workers load compliance checks lazily, `RequiresAttention` at `src/PeblClone.Domain/Workforce/Worker.cs:20-22` can trigger many queries. - Unbounded queries: dashboard currently reads all workers at `src/PeblClone.Application/Workforce/WorkforceDashboardService.cs:10`.

items.title: Why the EF adapter's DbContext should be scoped
items.body:
A `DbContext` tracks the entities it has loaded and is not safe to share between concurrent requests. Scoped means one instance per HTTP request, which matches that unit of work. The migration guidance says it directly: "Add a scoped DbContext, not a singleton adapter", and it points at today's singleton registration as the thing to change. The catalog's drill asks why singleton is fine for seed data but risky for a DbContext: seed data never changes, a DbContext holds per-request state.

Why the others are wrong:
- Keeping a singleton to preserve an in-memory cache reuses one DbContext across all requests, the risk the guide warns about.
- Migrations do not need the app's DbContext to live forever.
- The guide asks for scoped, not one context per query; transient would split one request's work across many contexts.

excerpts.quote: 2. Add a scoped DbContext, not a singleton adapter; current singleton evidence is `src/PeblClone.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:11`.
services.AddSingleton<IWorkforceReadModel, InMemoryWorkforceReadModel>();
**Drill:** Explain why singleton is okay for seed data but risky for DbContext.

items.title: Start here: PeblClone's layers and the architecture module
items.body:
PeblClone is a small demo of an employer-of-record (EOR) hiring app: an ASP.NET Core API, an Application layer with use cases, a Domain layer with records such as `Worker` and `Money`, an Infrastructure layer that holds seeded in-memory data, and a React web client. There is no database and no login yet. The course pages say so honestly, and many quizzes test that honesty.

This pack uses the module `docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/`. Read it in this order:

1. `02-data-model-and-persistence.md` - the in-memory stand-in and how EF Core would fit.
2. `03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md` - where input is checked today and what auth is missing.
3. `04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md` - async flow, and why a silent fallback is a reliability problem.
4. `05-pattern-catalog.md` - each pattern with a real example, why it works, and how it fails.
5. `06-architecture-critique.md` - strong choices, ranked risks, and a three-month plan.

Every claim in these pages carries a `path:line` anchor. Open it; the quizzes are about what the code at that line really does.

excerpts.quote: In this repo, the strongest boundary is API -> Application -> Domain with Infrastructure as an adapter
No EF Core `DbContext`, migration folder, connection string, or repository implementation was found.

readMore.why: The module's own reading list, including 01-boundaries-and-layers.md for the layer picture.
How the API, Application, Domain and Infrastructure projects depend on each other.

items.title: Why an Active worker with an open high-risk check is still flagged
items.body:
`RequiresAttention` is an OR of two conditions: the status is `NeedsAttention`, **or** any compliance check is unresolved and `High` risk. Changing the status to Active makes the first part false, but the open high-risk check makes the second part true, so the property returns true. The catalog keeps this rule as a computed property on `Worker` because "Attention logic has one source": every count or sort that asks a worker whether it needs attention gets the same answer.

Why the others are wrong:
- It does not read only `Status`; line 22 reads `ComplianceChecks`.
- Active does not override the checks, and no other code re-derives risk.
- The result does not depend on the dashboard service re-checking anything; the rule is on the record itself.

excerpts.quote: public bool RequiresAttention => Status == WorkerStatus.NeedsAttention || ComplianceChecks.Any(check => !check.IsResolved && check.RiskLevel is ComplianceRiskLevel.High);

**Problem:** Keep reusable invariant close to the data. **Real example:** `src/PeblClone.Domain/Workforce/Worker.cs:15-22` **Why it works:** Attention logic has one source. **Failure modes:** Expensive computed property over lazy-loaded data.

items.title: Why an HTML min attribute cannot protect the API
items.body:
`min="1000"` on the compensation input is a browser-side hint for people using the form. The API endpoint `POST /api/workforce/quotes` does not know or care whether a request came from that form: anyone can send the JSON with a tool like curl and a value of 0. The guide's "junior miss" is exactly this: the client check can be bypassed. The real rule lives on the server, in `HiringQuoteCalculator`, which rejects `MonthlyCompensation <= 0`.

Why the others are wrong:
- Browsers do honor `min` in the form UI; the problem is requests that never use the form.
- React does not strip `min`/`max` at build time; the attribute is right there in the JSX.
- The attribute's timing in the browser is irrelevant: the guide's point is that clients can skip the form.

excerpts.quote: <input min="1000" step="250" type="number"
Junior misses: HTML input minimum at `src/PeblClone.Web/src/features/QuoteBuilder.tsx:66-72` is not enough; clients can bypass it.
if (request.MonthlyCompensation <= 0) { return Result<HiringQuoteDto>.Failure("Monthly compensation must be greater than zero."); }

items.title: Why the UI's fallback quote math is a drift risk
items.body:
When `createQuote` fails to reach the API, `workforceApi.ts` computes a quote itself: its own employer-cost rates (0.21, 0.06, 0.09), its own platform fees and its own total. The server computes quotes in `HiringQuoteCalculator`. Two copies of the same pricing rules can drift apart: change one, forget the other, and users see a different price depending on whether the API answered. The critique rates this Medium and suggests removing the fallback math or generating mocks from a fixture.

Why the others are wrong:
- The fallback returns its quote to the UI; nothing posts it to the server.
- The critique does not mention negative fees or rounding bugs.
- The mock does use `employmentType`: it picks the rate and fee from it.

excerpts.quote: const employerCostRate = requestBody.employmentType === 'EmployerOfRecord' ? 0.21 : requestBody.employmentType === 'Contractor' ? 0.06 : 0.09;
Pricing duplicated in UI fallback

items.title: Ports, adapters and service lifetimes in plain words
items.body:
A **port** is an interface owned by the Application layer that says what data a use case needs, without saying where it comes from. Here that is `IWorkforceReadModel`. An **adapter** is a class in Infrastructure that implements the port. Today the only adapter is `InMemoryWorkforceReadModel`, which returns seeded data.

The two are joined in one place, the DI (dependency injection) registration in `DependencyInjection.cs`. When the app asks for an `IWorkforceReadModel`, the container hands out whatever class is registered there.

Registrations also choose a **lifetime**: singleton (one instance for the whole app), scoped (one per HTTP request) or transient (a new one every time it is asked for). As you read the persistence page and the pattern catalog, make two lists: which files would change if a real database replaced the seed data, and what each lifetime would mean for an object that holds a database connection. Then compare your lists with the catalog's "Failure modes" lines.

excerpts.quote: services.AddSingleton<IWorkforceReadModel, InMemoryWorkforceReadModel>();

items.title: Why missing [Authorize] is a possible risk, not a confirmed bug
items.body:
The guide confirms the facts: the controller has `[ApiController]` and `[Route]` but no `[Authorize]`, and `Program.cs` registers no auth services. It then labels the consequence carefully: "Possible risk, not a confirmed bug". This is a local demo; the risk becomes real if the API is exposed beyond local or demo use with real workforce, payroll and compliance data. Being precise about confidence is a senior skill this page is teaching.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Already leaking payroll data in production" claims evidence nobody has; the repo is a demo.
- CORS only tells browsers which sites may read responses; it does not authenticate callers, and the guide never calls it a protection.
- No ID parameters today does not make it safe: the dashboard returns payroll totals and worker names to anyone who calls it, and future detail endpoints will take IDs.

excerpts.quote: - Controller has `[ApiController]` and `[Route]`, not `[Authorize]`, at `src/PeblClone.Api/Controllers/WorkforceController.cs:6-7`. - Program registers controllers, CORS, health, OpenAPI, but not auth services at `src/PeblClone.Api/Program.cs:7-27`.
Possible risk, not a confirmed bug: if this API were exposed beyond local/demo use, workforce, payroll, and compliance data would need authentication, tenant scoping, and resource authorization.

readMore.why: The IDOR section on where resource IDs would enter.

items.title: Where an unavailable EOR hire is rejected
items.body:
`HiringQuoteCalculator.CalculateAsync` checks business rules in order: compensation above zero, a known country, then employer-of-record availability. For an EOR request in a country with `EmployerOfRecordAvailable` false, it returns a failed `Result` built with `.Failure(...)` and the message "Employer-of-record hiring is not available in ...". It returns a value; it does not throw. The controller then sees `!result.IsSuccess` and returns `BadRequest(new ProblemDetails { ... })`, so the caller gets a 400 with the message as `Detail`.

Why the others are wrong:
- The HTML `min` is about compensation, and it lives only in the form.
- `HiringQuoteRequest` has no attributes, so model binding has no rule to apply.
- No exception is thrown and no 500 is produced; the Result pattern exists to avoid exceptions for expected failures.

excerpts.quote: if (request.EmploymentType == EmploymentType.EmployerOfRecord && !country.EmployerOfRecordAvailable) { return Result<HiringQuoteDto>.Failure($"Employer-of-record hiring is not available in {country.Name}."); }

items.title: Where rules live: domain records, use cases and the controller
items.body:
The guides sort checks into three kinds: input shape (is the JSON well-formed and typed?), business rules (is this hire allowed in this country?) and authorization (may this caller see this data at all?). Each kind belongs in a different place.

Read these files with that question in mind:

- **Domain records** such as `Worker` and `Money`. Note which rules each record computes or enforces from its own data, and what happens when a rule is broken.
- **Application services** such as `HiringQuoteCalculator`. Note how a use case reports an expected failure to its caller.
- **The controller**, `WorkforceController`. Note what it does with each kind of result it receives.

Then ask where authorization lives today, and check the guide's answer. When you read each pattern in the catalog, note its "Failure modes" line; that line is usually the senior point.
